lessons.title: Effluent Treatment Basics
lessons.body:
Tanning uses a lot of water and chemicals. The dirty water that comes out is called effluent. If you dump it straight into a river or on the ground, it kills fish, plants, and makes people sick. So you must treat it first. This lesson shows you how to build a simple, low-cost effluent treatment system using locally available materials.

First, you need to separate your flows. Keep the beamhouse (soaking, liming, fleshing) wastewater separate from the tanning (chrome) wastewater. Beamhouse effluent is very alkaline and full of hair, flesh, and lime. Chrome effluent is acidic and contains chromium. Mixing them makes treatment harder. Use two different drains or buckets.

For beamhouse effluent, start with screening. Pass the water through a wire mesh or a woven sack to catch hair and flesh. Then let it settle in a settling tank â a simple pit lined with plastic or concrete, about 1 meter deep. Add lime to raise the pH to 11 or 12. This makes proteins and suspended solids settle to the bottom as sludge. After 4-6 hours, the clear water on top can go to a second tank. There, add carbon dioxide or just let it sit in the sun to lower the pH to 6-8. Then it can be used for irrigation or safely discharged.

For chrome effluent, the key is to raise the pH to 8-9 using soda ash or lime. This makes chromium hydroxide precipitate. Let it settle, then filter through sand and charcoal. The chromium sludge can be dried and sent to a licensed landfill or, better, recycled (see Lesson 2). The treated water can be reused in soaking or rinsing.

You can build a three-pit system: first pit for screening and settling, second for pH adjustment, third for polishing with sand and charcoal. Use a pH meter or pH paper (litmus) to check. Test every batch. Never discharge untreated effluent. In many African countries, it is illegal and you can be fined or closed down. Treating effluent protects your community, your workers, and your business.

lessons.title: Chrome Recovery and Recycling
lessons.body:
Chrome tanning is the most common way to make leather. But chromium is expensive and can pollute if wasted. A smart tanner recovers and reuses chrome. This lesson shows you how to recover chrome from spent tanning floats and shavings, saving money and reducing pollution.

First, collect your chrome tanning floats. After tanning, the leftover liquid contains about 1-3 grams of chromium per liter. Don't pour it away. Store it in a plastic tank. Also collect chrome shavings from trimming and buffing â they contain 2-4% chromium. You can sell shavings to a chrome recovery plant, or recover at your own workshop.

To recover chrome from float: heat the float to 60-70Â°C. Add sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) slowly while stirring until pH reaches 8.5-9.0. You will see a green-grey precipitate form â that's chromium hydroxide. Let it settle overnight. Filter through a cloth or fine mesh. Dry the sludge in the sun or in a low oven. You now have chrome hydroxide powder. To reuse it, dissolve it in sulfuric acid to make chrome tanning liquor again. Use 1 part recovered chrome to 3 parts fresh chrome for best results.

For shavings: you can burn them in a controlled incinerator to recover chromium oxide, but that's expensive. A simpler method: mix shavings with cement to make bricks, or use them as filler in rubber. But the best is to send them to a centralized recovery facility. In Africa, some tanneries in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa have such plants. If you are small, team up with other tanners to share a recovery unit.

Recovering chrome cuts your chemical bill by 20-30%. It also reduces the chromium in your effluent, making treatment easier. Always wear gloves, goggles, and a mask when handling chrome. Store recovered chrome in a dry, covered container. Never mix it with other waste. With practice, you can recover up to 90% of the chrome from your floats.

lessons.title: Solid Waste Management
lessons.body:
Tanning produces a lot of solid waste: trimmings, fleshings, hair, lime sludge, chrome shavings, and finished leather scraps. If you just throw them outside, they rot, smell, attract flies, and pollute groundwater. This lesson shows you how to manage each type of solid waste properly.

Start by sorting your waste at the source. Use separate bins or sacks for: (1) fleshings and trimmings (organic), (2) hair and lime sludge (alkaline), (3) chrome shavings (hazardous), (4) general rubbish. Label each bin clearly. Train your workers to put waste in the right bin.

Organic waste like fleshings and trimmings can be composted. Mix them with dry leaves, sawdust, or straw in a pile. Turn the pile every week. In 6-8 weeks, you get compost for your garden or to sell to farmers. You can also use fleshings to make animal feed after cooking and drying, but check local regulations.

Hair and lime sludge can be used to make building blocks. Mix 1 part dried sludge with 3 parts sand and 1 part cement. Add water and cast into blocks. Cure for 7 days. These blocks are strong and cheap. Alternatively, spread lime sludge on fields to raise soil pH, but only if it has no chromium.

Chrome shavings are hazardous. Never compost or burn them in the open. Store them in sealed plastic drums. Send them to a licensed hazardous waste facility or a chrome recovery plant. If you have a lot, invest in a small briquetting machine to compress them for easier transport.

Finally, reduce waste at the source. Cut hides carefully to minimize trimmings. Reuse offcuts for small items like keyrings, wallets, or patches. Sell unusable scraps to glue makers or paper mills. A clean workshop is a profitable workshop. Proper solid waste management keeps your workers healthy, your neighbors happy, and your business legal.

lessons.title: Air Emission Control
lessons.body:
Tanning can release bad smells and harmful gases. Hydrogen sulfide from liming smells like rotten eggs and is toxic. Ammonia from deliming irritates eyes and lungs. Dust from buffing and grinding contains chromium and leather particles. If you don't control these, your workers get sick and neighbors complain. This lesson shows you simple ways to control air emissions.

First, ventilate your work areas. Open windows and doors on opposite sides to create cross-breeze. Install roof vents or whirlybirds (wind-driven roof turbines) â they are cheap and need no electricity. For enclosed areas like the liming pit, use a local exhaust fan that pulls air outside. Place the fan near the source of fumes. Use ducting made from PVC pipes or metal sheets.

For hydrogen sulfide: keep the liming bath covered when not in use. Add a lid or plastic sheet. You can also add a small amount of hydrogen peroxide (0.1-0.2% of bath volume) to oxidize sulfide. Never mix liming waste with acid waste â that releases hydrogen sulfide gas instantly. Store them separately.

For ammonia: use a scrubber. A simple scrubber is a drum filled with water and a little sulfuric acid (pH 2-3). Pass the exhaust air through the water. Ammonia dissolves. Change the water every few days. You can also use a fine mist spray in the duct.

For dust: install a cyclone or bag filter on your buffing and grinding machines. A cyclone is a cone-shaped metal device that spins dust out of the air. A bag filter uses cloth bags to trap dust. Both can be made locally by a welder. Wear dust masks (N95 or better) when buffing. Keep floors wet or use a vacuum instead of sweeping to avoid raising dust.

Lastly, plant trees around your workshop. Trees act as natural filters and reduce smell. Choose fast-growing species like neem, eucalyptus, or moringa. Regular maintenance of your ventilation and scrubbers is key. Check fans, clean filters, and replace water. Good air quality protects your health and keeps you out of trouble with authorities.

lessons.title: Water Conservation Techniques
lessons.body:
Water is life, and in tanning it's also money. A typical tannery uses 30-50 liters of water per kilogram of hide. With water scarcity in many African regions, you can't afford to waste it. This lesson shows you practical ways to cut water use by 30-50% without hurting leather quality.

First, measure your water use. Install a simple water meter on your main line. Record daily readings. You can't manage what you don't measure. Identify the biggest users: soaking, liming, washing, and rinsing. Then target those.

Use batch washing instead of continuous overflow. In soaking, don't let water run continuously. Fill the drum, soak, then drain and refill only when needed. For washing after liming, use a three-stage counter-current rinse: fresh water enters the last rinse, then flows to the second, then to the first. This uses one-third the water of a single rinse.

Reuse water where possible. Soak water from clean hides can be used for the first soak of dirty hides. Rinse water from chrome tanning can be used for pickling or acidification. Final rinse water can be used for floor washing. But never reuse water that contains high levels of salt, lime, or chrome without treatment.

Fix leaks immediately. A dripping tap wastes 20 liters a day. Check pipes, valves, and drums regularly. Use trigger nozzles on hoses. Sweep floors instead of hosing them down. Use a bucket and mop for small spills.

Collect rainwater. Put gutters on your roof and direct water into a tank or lined pit. A 100 mÂ² roof can collect 1,000 liters from just 10 mm of rain. Use this for soaking or washing. In dry areas, this is a lifeline.

Finally, train your workers. Teach them to report leaks, use less water, and follow the batch methods. Put up signs: "Save Water â Every Drop Counts." With simple changes, you can save thousands of liters per week. That's money in your pocket and water for your community.

lessons.title: Sustainable Tanning Practices
lessons.body:
Sustainable tanning means making leather in a way that protects the environment, keeps workers healthy, and still makes a profit. It's not just about feeling good â it's about staying in business for the long term. This lesson brings together the best practices from all the previous lessons and adds a few more.

Start with cleaner production. That means preventing waste before it happens. Use fresh hides that are well-preserved to reduce salt and soaking. Use enzyme-assisted soaking and liming instead of harsh chemicals â enzymes work at lower temperatures and produce less waste. Recover and reuse chrome (Lesson 2). Use vegetable tanning for some products â it's slower but produces less toxic waste and is in demand for eco-friendly goods.

Choose your chemicals wisely. Buy from reputable suppliers who provide safety data sheets. Avoid banned substances like pentachlorophenol and azo dyes. Use biodegradable surfactants. Measure chemicals accurately â more is not better. Use a scale, not a scoop.

Save energy. Insulate your hot water tanks. Use solar water heaters if you can â many African countries have plenty of sun. Turn off lights and machines when not in use. Use energy-efficient motors.

Manage waste as a resource. Compost organic waste, recycle chrome, sell shavings to brick makers. Treat all effluent to safe levels before discharge or reuse. Keep records of your waste â how much, where it goes. This helps you improve and shows regulators you are responsible.

Train your workers regularly. Hold a 30-minute meeting every week to discuss safety, waste, and water. Encourage them to suggest improvements. Happy, healthy workers are more productive.

Finally, get certified. Look into certifications like LWG (Leather Working Group) or ISO 14001. They may seem far away, but you can start with simple steps: write down your procedures, set targets, and check your progress. Many buyers, especially in Europe and America, prefer sustainable leather. By adopting these practices, you can sell your leather at a premium and open new markets. Sustainability is not a cost â it's an investment in your future.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Environmental & Waste Management in Leather Making and Tanning

This practical reference is written for tannery owners, production managers, and technical supervisors working in African leather clusters â from Fes and Fez to Kano, Addis Ababa, Nairobi, and Durban. The goal is simple: keep your tannery compliant and profitable. Environmental management is not a cost centre; it is a licence to operate, a route to lower input costs, and increasingly a condition for accessing European and premium African markets. This module gives you the numbers, the sources, and the checklists you need to act today.

Why Effluent and Waste Management Is a Business Issue

Untreated tannery effluent carries high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), chromium, sulphides, and suspended solids. Discharging it into rivers or municipal drains triggers fines, closure orders, and community conflict. Conversely, well-managed tanneries recover chromium, reuse water, and sell or safely dispose of solid waste. In many African jurisdictions, environmental compliance is now enforced through national environmental management authorities â for example, Nigeria's NESREA, Kenya's NEMA, Ethiopia's EFCCC, and South Africa's DFFE. The practical reference below covers effluent treatment, chrome recovery, solid waste, air emissions, water conservation, and sustainable practices.

Effluent Treatment Basics: What You Must Measure

Effluent treatment is a sequence, not a single tank. Primary treatment removes solids and fats; secondary (biological) treatment reduces BOD and COD; tertiary treatment polishes for reuse or discharge. The critical parameters are pH, BOD, COD, total suspended solids (TSS), chromium, sulphide, and ammonia. In Africa, discharge limits vary by country, but most regulators align with WHO or national standards. The table below gives indicative limits and typical raw tannery values.

Table 1: Typical Raw Tannery Effluent vs. Indicative Discharge Limits
Parameter Raw Tannery Effluent (typical) Indicative Discharge Limit Business Implication
pH3â12 (variable)6.0â9.0Neutralisation required; prevents pipe corrosion
BODâ (mg/L)1,000â3,00030â50Biological treatment essential; high fines risk
COD (mg/L)2,000â8,000250â500Drives treatment cost; reduce at source
TSS (mg/L)1,000â4,00050â100Clarification and filtration needed
Chromium (mg/L)50â2000.5â2.0Recovery pays back; avoids toxic sludge
Sulphide (mg/L)100â5001â2Oxidation required; health hazard
Ammonia (mg/L)100â30010â50Nitrification needed; odour control

Sources: UNIDO (2011), Introduction to Treatment of Tannery Effluents; WHO (2006), Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater; national limits from NESREA (Nigeria), NEMA (Kenya), and DFFE (South Africa).

Chrome Recovery and Recycling: Turning Waste into Money

Chromium is the single most valuable recoverable input in a tannery. Spent chrome liquors can be recovered by precipitation, membrane filtration, or ion exchange. Recovery rates of 70â95% are achievable with simple settling and pH adjustment. Recovered chrome is reused in tanning, reducing purchase costs and sludge toxicity. In Ethiopia, Kenya, and Nigeria, tanneries that recover chrome report 15â25% savings on chrome sulphate purchases and lower sludge disposal costs. The table below summarises recovery methods.

Table 2: Chrome Recovery Methods â Performance and Cost Comparison
Method Recovery Rate CAPEX OPEX Best For
Precipitation (MgO/NaOH)70â85%LowLowSmall to medium tanneries
Membrane filtration85â95%HighMediumLarge tanneries, water reuse
Ion exchange90â98%HighMediumHigh-value finishing
Direct reuse (settling)50â70%Very lowVery lowArtisanal clusters

Sources: UNIDO (2011); FAO (1996), Pollution Control in the Leather Industry; Lofrano et al. (2013), Water Research.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHROME AND SULPHIDE HANDLING

Chromium VI is a known carcinogen and can cause severe skin ulceration and respiratory damage. Sulphide liquors release hydrogen sulphide (HâS) gas, which is lethal in confined spaces at concentrations above 500 ppm. Always:

  • Wear chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirators when handling chrome or sulphide baths.
  • Never mix acid and sulphide streams â this releases HâS gas.
  • Ventilate pits and tanks before entry; test for HâS and oxygen deficiency.
  • Store chrome and sulphide separately with bunded containment.
  • Provide emergency eyewash and shower within 10 seconds of workstations.

Solid Waste Management

Solid waste from tanneries includes fleshings, trimmings, shavings, sludge, and packaging. In Africa, fleshings and trimmings can be converted into protein hydrolysate, biogas, or animal feed. Chrome shavings must be segregated and either recovered or disposed of in licensed landfills. Sludge from effluent treatment, if chromium-free, can be composted or used in brick-making. The business case: waste-to-value reduces disposal fees and creates secondary revenue streams.

Air Emission Control

Air emissions come from ammonia (beamhouse), hydrogen sulphide (liming), solvents (finishing), and dust (buffing). Control measures include local exhaust ventilation, scrubbers for ammonia, and activated carbon filters for solvents. In dense African tannery clusters such as Fez and Kano, odour complaints are a major source of community friction. Simple fixes â covering tanks, extracting fumes, and scheduling liming operations â reduce complaints and regulatory attention.

Water Conservation Techniques

Water is the largest input in tanning â 30â50 mÂ³ per tonne of raw hide. Conservation measures include low-float drums, counter-current washing, reuse of soaking and rinsing water, and rainwater harvesting. A 20% reduction in water use directly cuts effluent volume and treatment costs. In water-scarce regions such as northern Nigeria and the Horn of Africa, water reuse is not optional â it is survival.

Sustainable Tanning Practices

Sustainable tanning means minimising chemical inputs, maximising recovery, and meeting buyer standards such as LWG (Leather Working Group) and ZDHC. African tanneries supplying European brands increasingly need audited environmental management systems (ISO 14001) and traceability. The payoff: access to premium markets, better prices, and resilience against regulatory shutdowns.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Segregate streams: Keep beamhouse (sulphide) and chrome liquors separate before treatment.
  2. Measure daily: Record pH, BOD, COD, TSS, chromium, and sulphide at inlet and outlet.
  3. Recover chrome: Install settling or precipitation; target 70%+ recovery.
  4. Neutralise: Adjust pH to 6â9 before discharge or reuse.
  5. Manage sludge: Dewater, test for chromium, and dispose only in licensed sites.
  6. Control air: Ventilate beamhouse and finishing; use scrubbers and carbon filters.
  7. Save water: Use low-float drums, counter-current washing, and rainwater harvesting.
  8. Document compliance: Keep records for regulators and buyers; pursue ISO 14001 or LWG.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • UNIDO â Introduction to Treatment of Tannery Effluents (2011)
  • FAO â Pollution Control in the Leather Industry
  • WHO â Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta and Greywater
  • Leather Working Group (LWG) â Audit Standards and Guidance
  • ZDHC â Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals Programme

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Leather Making and Tanning. Practical Reference module: Environmental and Waste Management. Always verify local discharge limits with your national environmental authority before discharging effluent.

quiz.q: Why should beamhouse effluent and chrome effluent be kept separate?
options: B) Mixing them makes treatment harder and can release toxic gas.
C) Chrome effluent is more valuable.
quiz.explanation: Mixing acidic chrome effluent with alkaline beamhouse effluent can release hydrogen sulfide gas and makes pH adjustment difficult.

quiz.q: What is the first step in treating beamhouse effluent?
options: B) Screen out hair and flesh.
quiz.explanation: Screening removes large solids like hair and flesh before further treatment.

quiz.q: What pH range should beamhouse effluent be raised to for settling proteins?
quiz.explanation: Adding lime to raise pH to 11-12 helps precipitate proteins and suspended solids.

quiz.q: How can you lower the pH of beamhouse effluent after settling?
options: C) Let it sit in the sun or add carbon dioxide.
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide or natural sunlight can lower pH to safe levels.

quiz.q: What chemical is used to precipitate chromium from chrome effluent?
quiz.explanation: Raising pH with soda ash or lime forms chromium hydroxide precipitate.

quiz.q: What is the typical chromium concentration in spent tanning float?
quiz.explanation: Spent chrome tanning floats contain about 1-3 grams of chromium per liter.

quiz.q: What temperature should you heat chrome float to for recovery?
quiz.explanation: Heating to 60-70Â°C helps the precipitation reaction proceed efficiently.

quiz.q: What is the precipitate formed when you add sodium hydroxide to chrome float?
quiz.explanation: Chromium hydroxide is the green-grey precipitate that can be dried and reused.

quiz.q: How can chrome shavings be reused in a simple way?
options: B) Mix with cement to make bricks.
C) Burn them in the open.
quiz.explanation: Chrome shavings can be mixed with cement and sand to make building blocks.

quiz.q: What percentage of chrome can be recovered from floats with good practice?
quiz.explanation: With proper recovery methods, up to 90% of chrome can be recovered.

quiz.q: Why should you sort solid waste at the source?
options: A) To make it look neat.
B) To reduce the amount of waste.
C) To handle each type properly and avoid contamination.
quiz.explanation: Sorting ensures hazardous waste like chrome shavings is not mixed with compostable waste.

quiz.q: Which of these is considered organic solid waste in tanning?
quiz.explanation: Fleshings and trimmings are organic and can be composted.

quiz.q: How long does it take to make compost from fleshings?
quiz.explanation: With weekly turning, compost is ready in about 6-8 weeks.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to dispose of chrome shavings?
options: A) Burn them in the open.
B) Throw them in the river.
C) Send to a licensed hazardous waste facility.
quiz.explanation: Chrome shavings are hazardous and must go to a licensed facility or recovery plant.

quiz.q: How can you reduce solid waste at the source?
options: A) Cut hides carefully to minimize trimmings.
quiz.explanation: Careful cutting reduces offcuts and waste.

quiz.q: What gas smells like rotten eggs and is toxic?
quiz.explanation: Hydrogen sulfide is produced during liming and is highly toxic.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to control hydrogen sulfide in the liming pit?
options: B) Keep the pit covered and add hydrogen peroxide.
C) Blow air into the pit.
quiz.explanation: Covering the pit and adding small amounts of hydrogen peroxide oxidizes sulfide.

quiz.q: What is a scrubber used for?
options: B) Removing ammonia from exhaust air.
quiz.explanation: A scrubber passes exhaust air through water or acid solution to dissolve ammonia.

quiz.q: What should you wear when buffing leather to protect from dust?
options: A) A dust mask (N95 or better).
quiz.explanation: Dust masks prevent inhalation of chromium and leather particles.

quiz.q: Why plant trees around a tannery?
options: A) To provide shade for workers.
B) To act as natural filters for air emissions.
quiz.explanation: Trees help absorb odors and filter dust from the air.

quiz.q: How much water does a typical tannery use per kg of hide?
quiz.explanation: A typical tannery uses 30-50 liters of water per kilogram of hide processed.

quiz.q: What is a three-stage counter-current rinse?
options: A) Rinsing with hot water three times.
B) Using fresh water in the last stage, then reusing it in earlier stages.
C) Adding soap to each rinse.
quiz.explanation: Counter-current rinsing reuses water from later stages in earlier stages, saving water.

quiz.q: How much water can a dripping tap waste per day?
quiz.explanation: A dripping tap can waste about 20 liters of water per day.

quiz.q: What is a good way to collect rainwater for tanning?
options: A) Dig a pit in the ground.
B) Use gutters on the roof and direct to a tank.
C) Place buckets in the yard.
D) Use a hose from the river.
quiz.explanation: Gutters and a storage tank capture rainwater from rooftops.

quiz.q: How much water can a 100 mÂ² roof collect from 10 mm of rain?
quiz.explanation: 100 mÂ² x 0.01 m = 1 mÂ³ = 1,000 liters.

quiz.q: What is cleaner production?
options: B) Preventing waste before it is created.
C) Using more chemicals to speed up tanning.
quiz.explanation: Cleaner production focuses on reducing waste at the source rather than treating it later.

quiz.q: Which tanning method produces less toxic waste?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable tanning uses natural tannins and produces less toxic effluent.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pentachlorophenol?
options: B) It is banned and toxic.
quiz.explanation: Pentachlorophenol is a banned hazardous substance.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using solar water heaters in tanning?
options: A) They are cheap to buy.
B) They reduce energy costs and are environmentally friendly.
C) They heat water faster than electricity.
quiz.explanation: Solar water heaters save money on energy and reduce carbon footprint.

quiz.q: What certification can help you sell sustainable leather at a premium?
quiz.explanation: LWG certification is recognized in the leather industry for sustainability.
